official_sources.title: Environment Agency LiDAR vertical accuracy FAQ
official_sources.authority: Environment Agency / Defra Data Services Platform
official_sources.finding: EA specification requires absolute height error below ±15 cm RMSE versus ground truth and expects relative height error (random error) no more than ±5 cm.
official_sources.limitation: ±15 cm RMSE and ±5 cm relative error are specification/QA quantities, not a measured parcel-specific uncertainty interval.

official_sources.title: Environment Agency LiDAR Ground Truth Surveys
official_sources.authority: Environment Agency / Defra Data Services Platform
official_sources.finding: Ground-truth points are independently surveyed at ±3 cm RMSE; timestamped LiDAR surveys are compared against them using RMSE, standard deviation and random error, and must meet stated QA thresholds.
official_sources.limitation: Ground-truth point accuracy and LiDAR acceptance thresholds are distinct uncertainty components and cannot be collapsed into one number without a model.

official_sources.title: LIDAR DTM Time Stamped Tiles
official_sources.finding: Time-stamped DTM is available at 25 cm, 50 cm, 1 m and 2 m raster resolution while all LiDAR data is stated as ±15 cm RMSE vertical accuracy.
official_sources.limitation: Raster cell size and vertical accuracy are separate properties; finer cells do not imply proportionally smaller vertical RMSE.

official_sources.title: LIDAR Composite DTM 1m
official_sources.finding: The 1 m composite states that contributing LiDAR surveys have ±15 cm RMSE vertical accuracy and provides survey-index metadata for location-specific source lineage.
official_sources.limitation: The ±15 cm statement is survey-level input quality, not a guarantee that every derived composite cell has an independently measured ±15 cm parcel-specific error.

official_sources.title: LIDAR Composite DTM 2m
official_sources.authority: Environment Agency / Defra Data Services Platform
official_sources.finding: The 2 m composite uses merged/resampled surveys and states ±15 cm RMSE vertical accuracy for LiDAR inputs while newest/best-resolution sources can be selected.
official_sources.limitation: Resampling and mixed survey lineage add processing/provenance considerations not represented by the survey RMSE alone.

official_sources.title: LIDAR Composite DTM 10m
official_sources.authority: Environment Agency / Defra Data Services Platform
official_sources.finding: The 10 m composite is a much coarser raster yet still reports the source LiDAR vertical accuracy as ±15 cm RMSE.
official_sources.limitation: Matching survey RMSE across different cell sizes demonstrates that nominal raster resolution must not be used as a vertical-accuracy proxy.

official_sources.title: EA LiDAR point-density guidance
official_sources.authority: Environment Agency / Defra Data Services Platform
official_sources.finding: EA relates point density to requested surface-model resolution and notes DTM density under vegetation can differ from DSM density; point clouds are irregular and described by density rather than raster resolution.
official_sources.limitation: Point density, DTM grid resolution and vertical accuracy are different quality dimensions.

official_sources.title: EA projection and geoid-model guidance
official_sources.authority: Environment Agency / Defra Data Services Platform
official_sources.finding: EA states elevations are AODN/ODN and that geoid models changed over time; post-26-Aug-2016 surveys use OSGM15 while time-stamped metadata identifies the model used for each survey.
official_sources.limitation: Vertical transformation model uncertainty and survey measurement error must remain separately attributed.

official_sources.title: Ordnance Survey OSGM15 accuracy FAQ
official_sources.finding: OS states OSGM15 accuracy is 8 mm RMS (1 standard error) for mainland Britain and relative model error over a 10 km extent is at most a few millimetres.
official_sources.limitation: OSGM15 model error is not the same quantity as EA LiDAR survey RMSE or final parcel-height-difference uncertainty.

official_sources.title: USGS topographic data quality levels
official_sources.finding: USGS quality levels list vertical RMSE, pulse spacing/density and DEM cell size as separate requirements; for example different quality levels can share cell size while differing in RMSE.
official_sources.limitation: USGS requirements are not EA acceptance criteria; they are used here to reinforce the general distinction between spatial resolution and vertical accuracy.

official_sources.title: USGS adoption of updated accuracy standards
official_sources.finding: USGS documents 2024 positional-accuracy standard changes including terminology changes and removal of the former 95% confidence-level formulation from its revised Lidar Base Specification table.
official_sources.limitation: Historical RMSE-to-95% conventions must not be imported blindly into a current EA result or mixed across standards versions.

official_sources.title: USGS Lidar Base Specification glossary
official_sources.finding: The glossary records legacy/defined relationships such as ACCz = 1.9600 × RMSEz at 95% confidence and distinguishes absolute/network/local/relative accuracy concepts.
official_sources.limitation: This relationship is standard- and assumption-dependent and must be version-labelled; it is not an automatic conversion for EA ±15 cm RMSE.

official_sources.title: NIST combined standard uncertainty
official_sources.finding: NIST combines standard uncertainty components through the law of propagation of uncertainty, with covariances included as appropriate; simple RSS is valid only under the corresponding assumptions.
official_sources.limitation: A height-difference uncertainty budget must not blindly RSS correlated components such as common vertical-datum effects.

official_sources.title: NIST law of propagation of uncertainty
official_sources.finding: NIST expresses a derived measurand as a function of input quantities and propagates standard uncertainties with sensitivity coefficients and covariance terms.
official_sources.limitation: The exact functional model and correlations for parcel max-minus-min must be defined before computing a numerical combined uncertainty.

official_sources.title: NIST Type A uncertainty
official_sources.finding: NIST Type A evaluation uses statistical analysis of observations, such as standard deviations, least squares or ANOVA, to quantify random effects.
official_sources.limitation: Static published specifications are not Type A observations of the target parcel unless target-specific repeated evidence actually exists.

official_sources.title: NIST Type B uncertainty
official_sources.finding: NIST Type B evaluation can use prior data, experience, manufacturer specifications, calibration reports and uncertainties assigned to reference data.
official_sources.limitation: Published EA/OS accuracy statements can feed a Type B-style budget only after their statistical meaning and coverage are interpreted correctly.

official_sources.title: NIST uncertainty-component classification and covariance
official_sources.finding: NIST represents uncertainty components as standard deviations and explicitly characterizes correlations through covariances or correlation coefficients.
official_sources.limitation: Common-mode survey, datum or transformation effects in max/min values require a correlation ledger rather than implicit independence.

official_sources.title: NIST expanded uncertainty and coverage factors
official_sources.finding: NIST defines expanded uncertainty U = k uc and notes k≈2 gives approximately 95% coverage under suitable normal-distribution assumptions.
official_sources.limitation: A confidence percentage must never be attached without recording the coverage factor and the assumptions supporting it.

official_sources.title: NIST reporting uncertainty
official_sources.finding: NIST reporting guidance calls for reporting expanded uncertainty together with the coverage factor k, or reporting combined standard uncertainty.
official_sources.limitation: The website must distinguish source specification, standard uncertainty, expanded uncertainty, confidence/coverage and readiness score.

official_sources.title: ISO 19157 geographic data quality
official_sources.finding: ISO 19157 establishes principles and measures for describing, evaluating and reporting geographic-data quality, but explicitly does not define minimum acceptable quality levels.
official_sources.limitation: Quality metadata and acceptance criteria must be kept explicit; an internal readiness percentage is not a standardized positional-accuracy measure.
